theme: The promise; the Magnificat; the Benedictus
readingInstruction: Read Luke 1:1-80. Luke begins with a careful preface, then tells of two miraculous births: John to an old priest and his wife, and Jesus to a young virgin. Read Mary’s song (1:46-55) and Zechariah’s song (1:68-79) aloud, slowly.
settingTheScene: Luke was a physician and a traveling companion of Paul. He was not an eyewitness, and he says so. He investigated everything carefully and wrote an orderly account for a man named Theophilus, so that he might know the certainty of what he had been taught. Luke also wrote the book of Acts, and together the two books make up about a quarter of the New Testament. Luke is especially interested in the Holy Spirit, in prayer, in women, in the poor and outcast, and in good news that reaches the Gentiles. The Gospel opens in the temple in Jerusalem, in the dusty hill country, and in a small town of Galilee, and it begins with songs.
observation: “It seemed good to me also, having followed all things closely for some time past, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus” (1:3).
“And he will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even from his mother’s womb” (1:15).
“The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the child to be born will be called holy, the Son of God” (1:35).
“For nothing will be impossible with God” (1:37).
“Behold, I am the servant of the Lord; let it be to me according to your word” (1:38).
“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior” (1:46-47).
“He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty” (1:52-53).
“Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, for he has visited and redeemed his people” (1:68).
interpretation:
Luke tells us at the outset what kind of book this is. It is history, researched and arranged with care. The faith is not built on rumor. It is built on events that happened, which witnesses saw and Luke investigated.

The first scene is in the temple. An old priest named Zechariah is told that his barren wife Elizabeth will bear a son who will go before the Lord “in the spirit and power of Elijah,” to turn hearts and prepare a people. Zechariah doubts and is made silent. The Gospel begins where the Old Testament ended, with Malachi’s promise of Elijah, and with silence broken.

Then the angel comes to Mary, a young woman in Nazareth, and Luke gives us one of the great statements of the incarnation. The Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the child will be the Son of God. Mary’s response is a model of faith: “Let it be to me according to your word.” She does not understand how, but she trusts.

Mary visits Elizabeth, and the unborn John leaps. Then Mary sings the Magnificat, which is built from the songs of the Old Testament, especially Hannah’s. It is a song about reversal. God lifts up the lowly, feeds the hungry, and sends the rich away empty. It is also a song about promise kept: God has helped his servant Israel, “as he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his offspring forever.” The salvation Mary sings about is both spiritual and concrete, and it will turn the world’s order upside down.

The chapter ends with Zechariah’s song, the Benedictus. His tongue is loosed, and he is filled with the Spirit and praises God for visiting and redeeming his people, for raising up a horn of salvation in the house of David, and for remembering his holy covenant. He closes with the image of the sunrise from on high, giving light to those in darkness and guiding feet into the way of peace. A new day is dawning.
connection: Genesis 18:14 asked, “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” and Luke 1:37 answers it. 1 Samuel 2:1-10 is Hannah’s song, which stands behind Mary’s. Malachi 4:5-6 promised Elijah, and Luke 1:17 shows John fulfilling it. 2 Samuel 7:12-16 is the promise to David that Gabriel echoes in 1:32-33. Isaiah 7:14 and 9:6-7 are in the background. John 1:14 says the Word became flesh. Galatians 4:4 says God sent forth his Son, born of woman.
application:
Read the Magnificat aloud. Which line speaks to you most, and why?

Think of a promise from God that seems impossible. Pray Mary’s answer: “Let it be to me according to your word.”

Notice how many people in this chapter are ordinary and humble. Thank God that he works through those the world overlooks.
prayerPrompts: Say to God, “Let it be to me according to your word,” and tell him what that means for you.
Thank him for keeping his promises to Abraham and David.
Praise him, as Mary did, in your own words.
